content.title: About
content.content: Canned spinach consists of cooked spinach leaves that have been heat‑treated and sealed in a jar with added fat. The product is ready to eat, retains most of its nutrients, and has a soft, tender texture.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Spinach belongs to the Amaranthaceae family and is grown in temperate climates worldwide.
Canning allows spinach to be stored for several years without loss of flavor.
Added fat enhances the absorption of fat‑soluble vitamins A, D, E, and K.
Spinach is a staple in Mediterranean cuisine, often appearing in casseroles, pastas, and dips.
Many canned spinach products are labeled “no added salt” when salt is omitted.

items.title: Rich in vitamin K
items.content: Vitamin K is essential for blood clotting and bone health.

items.title: Source of vitamin A
items.content: Vitamin A supports vision, immune function, and skin integrity.

items.title: Contains iron
items.content: Iron is needed for oxygen transport in the blood.

items.title: Provides dietary fiber
items.content: Fiber promotes normal digestion and a feeling of fullness.

items.title: Antioxidant properties
items.content: Phytonutrients in spinach help combat free radicals.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: If salt is added, total sodium intake should be monitored.

items.title: Leaf‑vegetable allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience an allergic reaction to spinach.

items.title: Oxalates
items.content: Spinach contains oxalates, which can contribute to kidney‑stone formation in susceptible people.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Canned spinach can be eaten cold in salads, added to soups, stews, pasta dishes, or used as a filling for pies and quiches. Shake the jar before opening to distribute the fat evenly.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store unopened jars in a cool, dry place away from direct sunlight. After opening, keep the spinach in a sealed container in the refrigerator and consume within 3–4 days.
